transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (Avalon - Head of ML), Rajiv Patel (Avalon - Infra Lead), Lena Zhou (Avalon - Security)

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick intro, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Ethan, our solutions engineer. How's the audio?
[00:09] Sofia (Avalon): Good here, can you hear me fine.
[00:12] Rajiv (Avalon): Yup, good.
[00:14] Ethan (SE): Great. We'd like to focus on latency and throughput today, and make sure we capture your p95 targets and concurrency patterns so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:25] Sofia: Yeah, that's the main thing. We're planning to move some customer-facing flows to real-time summarization and chat — strict SLOs. For small, interactive requests we want p95 under about 300ms, ideally 200 to 250ms, at 50-100 concurrent users. For longer streaming responses (docs -> summarization) we care about token/sec and stable tail latency.
[00:48] Ethan: Helpful. When you say 50-100 concurrent users, is that concurrent open connections, or active token-generation streams?
[00:55] Sofia: Active generation streams. So if 80 users are generating simultaneously, that's 80 concurrent generation streams. Typical prompt+response is 128 tokens input, expecting 256 tokens out on average.
[01:12] Maya: Got it. And what level of throughput do you need overall? e.g., peak requests per second or tokens per second across the cluster?
[01:20] Rajiv: Peak qps around 120 request/sec during trading hours for some flows, but the critical one is the chat path — we measure by concurrent generation. So in terms of tokens/sec, rough back-of-envelope: 120 rps * 256 tokens = ~30k tokens/sec at peak; but simultaneous constraint is the p95 for single-stream latency.
[01:40] Ethan: OK, that's a useful baseline. For hosted, our latency depends on model size and context length; smaller models and quantized variants hit lower p95. For dedicated, you can guarantee capacity and lower noisy-neighbor variance. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control but requires more ops.
[02:02] Sofia: We want to understand tradeoffs — we prefer hosted if it meets p95, but security requires SOC2 + VPC peering for production data. If hosted can't meet p95 for the chat use case, we'll look at dedicated pools.
[02:20] Lena (Security): On security, we'll need SOC2 Type II, ISO27001, and KMS/HSM for key management; audit logs and per-request provenance. Can you share docs?
[02:30] Maya: Absolutely, we'll send SOC2 and ISO reports and our KMS integration guide. We'll include retention and audit log details.
[02:38] Rajiv: Also need to know about KV cache behavior — if you do prefix caching can you evict per-tenant? We can't have cross-tenant leaks.
[02:48] Ethan: Yes, tenant-isolated KV cache and TTLs; we can pin caches to dedicated pools. Apologies if I say KV cash later in the call — our transcription sometimes says cash.
[02:58] Sofia: ha, noted.

[03:10] [03:10] Ethan: Let's talk numbers. For a 256->512 token generation on a 4k context model, on a single GPU we see X token/sec. (interruption) But to be practical, for p95 under 300ms at concurrency 80, you'd likely need dedicated capacity or a hosted premium tier with reserved instances.
[03:35] Rajiv: Can you quantify — how many GPUs or what instance size would that be? We need cost estimates.
[03:42] Ethan: Rough ballpark: if we target p95 ~200-250ms for short completions (<=256 tokens) and streaming enabled, you'd be looking at NVL-optimized instances or A100-class throughput; approx 8–12 concurrent streams per GPU at that latency for heavy models. So for 80 concurrent streams, roughly 7–10 GPUs. Those numbers shift with quantization and model variant.
[04:08] Maya: For benchmarking, we'll send a spreadsheet with test scenarios: short chat (128/256), medium summarization (512-1024), long streaming (2k-8k context) and concurrency sweeps. We want token/sec, p50/p95/p99 and end-to-end streaming latency.
[04:25] Sofia: That would be great. Also, what about streaming granularity — chunk size impacts p95; we prefer smaller chunks for faster first-byte but might increase per-token overhead.
[04:36] Ethan: Correct. We typically default to 64-token chunks for streaming, but settable. We can test 16/32/64 to see impact on p95 and throughput.

[04:50] [04:50] Rajiv: For private deployment, our ops team is open to on-prem if latency is critical. But on-prem ops is heavy; we want to know the delta in latency vs dedicated in-cloud.
[05:02] Ethan: For on-prem with direct PCIe-connected GPUs and local network, tail latency can be lower by 20-40% compared to multi-tenant cloud; but you trade off scalability and maintenance. Dedicated pools in cloud with reserved instances get closer if you reserve capacity and isolate tenancy.
[05:22] Lena: Any differences in observability for private vs dedicated vs hosted? We need full traces and token-level cost breakdowns.
[05:30] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. For private, we can push logs to your SIEM and enable SAML SSO and RBAC. We'll include screenshots in the deck.

[05:47] [05:47] Sofia: For the benchmark we want p95 target of 200ms for interactive chat (<=256 tokens) at 80 concurrency as a stretch; acceptable is 300ms. For summarization (512-1024 tokens) we want p95 under 1.2s. For long streaming (2k+ context) we want sustained token/sec of at least 15k across the cluster during peak.
[06:12] Ethan: Helpful specifics. When you say 15k tokens/sec cluster-wide, is that across the cluster or per-GPU?
[06:18] Rajiv: Cluster-wide. Per-GPU numbers would be useful for sizing.
[06:22] Ethan: We'll include per-GPU token/sec estimates in the spreadsheet. Note that token/sec depends heavily on sequence length and attention optimizations; 4-bit quantized models increase tokens/sec by ~1.5–2x in many cases.
[06:39] Maya: Do you have any hard limits on network egress or data residency?
[06:44] Lena: Data residency needs to stay in us-east-1 and logs stored for seven years for audit purposes.
[06:50] Maya: We can provision regionally-hosted capacity and longer retention as an add-on.

[07:00] [07:00] Ethan: A note about streaming first-byte latency vs completion latency: we can optimize for first-byte (faster perceived latency) by reducing chunk sizes and prioritizing scheduling; completion p95 will still be a function of tokens generated. For interactive UIs first-byte often matters more.
[07:20] Sofia: First-byte is super important for chat. If the first token arrives fast, UX looks snappy, even if total completion is a bit longer.
[07:28] Ethan: Exactly. We'll test for first-byte p50/p95 as well.

[07:40] [07:40] Rajiv: On pricing, is hosted billed per-token; dedicated is reserved monthly? We need a sense of unit economics to compare to running our own infra.
[07:49] Maya: Yes, hosted is usage-based per-token. Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commitments — typically cheaper per-token at scale. Private has platform licensing and support fees plus ops. We'll follow up with a pricing comparison table for your expected token volumes.

[08:05] [08:05] Sofia: Any benchmarks with real-time streaming for finance workloads? We often have short templates with dynamic entities — low latency, variable token counts.
[08:15] Ethan: We have internal benchmarks and some customer case studies in fintech; we'll share anonymized results and a small reference app. The spreadsheet will include a sample streaming harness you can run against our hosted pilot endpoint.
[08:29] Lena: For compliance, can the hosted pilot be VPC peered?
[08:33] Maya: Yes, we offer VPC peering for hosted pilots under certain conditions; otherwise we can spin up a dedicated private pilot. We'll clarify in the follow-up.

[08:44] [08:44] Sofia: On concurrency, do you support autoscaling for dedicated pools to handle spikes (e.g., market open)?
[08:51] Ethan: Yes, configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity options. For strict SLOs we recommend a baseline reserved capacity plus burst headroom. 

[09:05] [09:05] Rajiv: Do you do warmup/preheat for model caches to avoid cold-start latencies?
[09:10] Ethan: Yes; we support pre-warming, pinned model residency, and KV cache priming for known prefixes. We'll include warmup scripts in the benchmark package.

[09:24] [09:24] Maya: Any blockers or questions on your side about tests?
[09:27] Sofia: We'll need the test harness and sample prompts by Monday, and ideally pilot credentials same week. Also want to validate SLOs with a small alpha group.
[09:38] Maya: We'll try to get the spreadsheet and pilot access out Monday. Ethan will configure the streaming tests.

[09:45] [09:45] Ethan: Quick technical thing — for token/sec measurements, we recommend three measurement axes: cold start, steady-state streaming, and tail latency under concurrency sweeps. We'll provide scripts that measure tokens/sec and emit p50/p95/p99.
[09:59] Rajiv: Good. Also include network emulation for flaky mobile connections; that'll affect perceived latencies.
[10:06] Ethan: Can do.

[10:12] [10:12] Lena: Regarding encryption, we require customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-KMS) for production. Support for HSM would be ideal.
[10:20] Maya: We support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private; hosted supports KMS integration with managed keys — we'll note exact HSM capabilities in the security pack.

[10:32] [10:32] Sofia: Any other pitfalls people typically see in these benchmarks?
[10:36] Ethan: A few: 1) mixing prompt lengths in the same test can skew token/sec; run separate buckets. 2) streaming chunk size affects first-byte latency. 3) model warmup and KV priming matter a lot for tail. 4) instrumentation — make sure you collect both server and client-side timings.
[10:57] Maya: We'll include best-practices in the spreadsheet.

[11:05] [11:05] Sofia: Great. Can you also include recommendations on quantization levels and likely impact on quality? We want to be careful about 4-bit vs 8-bit tradeoffs.
[11:15] Ethan: Yes. We'll annotate recommended quantization profiles per workload; for chat we often recommend 4-bit/llm-int8-ish variants for inference cost savings with minimal quality regressions, but we'll include A/B eval steps.
[11:29] Rajiv: Timeline-wise, we want to run a 2-week pilot in April and make a decision in May.
[11:36] Maya: Good — we'll aim to have the pilot provisioned early April pending your sign-off.

[11:45] [11:45] Maya: Quick recap of action items: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and test harness, Ethan will set up streaming configs for 8k context and chunk size variants, Avalon to share prompts and infra diagram, Redwood to share SOC2/ISO and KMS docs and pricing.
[12:05] Sofia: That matches our notes. Thanks, everyone.
[12:09] Rajiv: Thanks.
[12:11] Lena: Thanks all.
[12:13] Maya: We'll follow up with the materials Monday. Bye.

(Transcript end)
